A suffering woman's voice corrects a priest

Three people misread Hannah in this chapter. Her rival provokes her (verse 6). Her husband asks if he is not better than ten sons (verse 8). The priest takes her silent prayer for drunkenness (verses 13–14). In verses 15–16 she corrects him firmly and with respect. Eli changes his charge into a blessing (verse 17). Verse 18 says her face was no longer sad, before any child is born.
The household tests the meaning of sacred office

The sons’ sin is plain in verses 13–17 and 22. Eli’s part is harder to see. He does speak to them (verses 23–25), but with words only. Verse 29 charges him with honoring his sons above God. It also says “yourselves,” so he shares in what they took. Verse 30 states the rule that follows: the LORD honors those who honor him. Between these scenes the text keeps noting Samuel’s growth (verses 18, 21, 26).
Receiving a call includes speaking difficult words

Samuel’s first message is a judgment on the man who raised him. Verse 15 says he was afraid to tell it. Eli himself taught the boy how to listen (verse 9). Eli also insists on hearing every word (verse 17). In verse 18 Samuel hides nothing, and Eli accepts the sentence. The text does not report that he changed anything afterward. Verse 19 says the LORD let none of Samuel’s words fail.
A sacred object cannot secure a chosen outcome

The elders ask a good question in verse 3: why did the LORD defeat us? They do not wait for an answer. They send for the ark so that “it” may save them. The priests who come with it are the two condemned in 2:34. The shout in verse 5 is confident, and the loss is far worse. Chapter 7:3–4 later shows what was missing here. The people had not put away their other gods.
Power is questioned outside Israel's territory

The Philistines won the battle and placed the ark as a trophy (verse 2). No Israelite soldier or priest is present in this chapter. The LORD acts alone in the enemy’s own temple. In verse 7 the men of Ashdod read the events correctly. His hand is heavy on them and on Dagon. Their answer is to send the problem to the next town (verse 8). Each move spreads the harm (verses 9–12).
The return includes a stated test of cause

The Philistine priests design a test in verses 7–9. Nursing cows that never pulled a cart should turn back to their calves. If they leave, something stronger than instinct is moving them. Verse 9 names the other option honestly: it may have been chance. Verse 12 reports the result, with the cows lowing all the way. The ark is no safer for Israel’s own town (verse 19). Beth Shemesh asks who can stand before this holy God (verse 20).
A victory becomes a named act of remembrance

The name Ebenezer first appears in 4:1, where Israel camped before defeat. There the people fetched the ark and shouted. Here they put away their gods and confess (verses 4 and 6). They ask Samuel to pray; they do not ask for an object (verse 8). The same enemy is driven back. In verse 12 Samuel marks the place with a stone and a name. His words are modest: the LORD has helped “until now.”
A king can take what a people needs

The elders have a real complaint: Samuel’s sons are corrupt (verse 3). Their fix is to be “like all the nations” (verse 5). Samuel’s warning repeats one phrase again and again: “he will take.” The list runs from sons and daughters to fields and flocks (verses 11–17). Verse 17 ends it: “you will be his servants.” The LORD once brought Israel out of service to a king in Egypt. The people hear all this and still choose it (verses 19–20).
A servant opens the way to royal appointment

Saul is about to give up the search in verse 5. The unnamed servant knows about the man of God (verse 6). The servant also has the quarter shekel (verse 8). Saul does not even recognize Samuel at the gate (verse 18). Verses 15–16 show the other side of the story. The LORD had already told Samuel when the man would come. Lost donkeys and a servant’s idea bring Saul to that meeting.
Public selection does not erase uncertainty

Saul already has the oil, the signs, and a changed heart (verses 1–9). When the lot falls on him, he cannot be found. The people must ask the LORD where he is (verse 22). The text gives no reason for his hiding. It may be modesty or fear, and the chapter leaves that open. Samuel presents him by his height (verses 23–24). In verse 19 Samuel has just said that Israel rejected God that day.
Victory gives Saul a chance to restrain revenge

In 10:27 some men asked how Saul could save them. After the victory the people want those men put to death (verse 12). Saul now has the power and the public support to do it. Verse 13 records his refusal. He gives the credit for the rescue to the LORD, not to himself. This is Saul at his best: moved by the Spirit and restrained in victory. Later chapters should be read against this one.
The outgoing leader invites public examination

In 8:11–17 Samuel warned that a king would “take.” In verse 3 he asks whose ox or donkey he himself has taken. The people clear him before the LORD and the new king (verses 4–5). His clean record becomes the standard the king will be measured by. Verses 14–15 place king and people under the same condition. Samuel gives up rule but not his work. Verse 23 says he would sin if he stopped praying for them.
Pressure reveals competing accounts of responsibility

Saul’s answer in verse 11 lists three things he saw. The people were scattering, Samuel was late, and the Philistines had gathered. Verses 5–8 confirm that all three were true. His conclusion follows in verse 12: “I forced myself.” Every reason concerns what he could see. None concerns the instruction in 10:8 to wait. Samuel’s reply in verse 13 names only that: Saul did not keep the command.
The people challenge a royal sentence

Saul’s oath in verse 24 speaks of “my enemies.” It weakens his own army on the day of victory. Jonathan says so plainly in verse 29: his father has troubled the land. The hunger leads the soldiers to break the law about blood (verse 32). Saul then swears twice more that the guilty will die (verses 39 and 44). In verse 45 the people overrule their king. They say Jonathan worked “with God” that day.
Claiming a sacred purpose does not end the dispute

Saul’s account changes as Samuel presses him. In verse 13 he says he has done what the LORD commanded. In verse 15 “they” spared the animals, for sacrifice. In verses 20–21 he obeyed, but “the people” took the plunder. Verse 9 had said that Saul and the people spared them together. He speaks of “the LORD your God” three times (verses 15, 21, 30). In verse 30 he still asks to be honored before the elders.
Music belongs inside the court

In verses 13–14 the Spirit comes on David and leaves Saul. Saul’s own servants then bring the newly anointed man to court (verse 18). Saul loves him and makes him armor bearer (verse 21). He does not know what Samuel did in Bethlehem. David’s first service to the king is to ease him, not replace him. He plays a harp (verse 23); the Egyptian harp shown is only a comparison. The text says the troubling spirit was “from God” and explains no more.
The chosen tools change the contest

Verses 5–7 list Goliath’s armor and weapons piece by piece. Saul answers in kind in verse 38 with a helmet and coat of mail. Saul is Israel’s tallest man (9:2) and its king, yet he stays back. David says he cannot go in gear he has not tested (verse 39). In verse 40 he takes a shepherd’s tools. His speech in verses 45–47 gives the reason. The LORD does not save by sword and spear.
Public praise turns achievement into a royal threat

The song praises Saul too, but he hears only the comparison. In verse 8 he leaps from a song to the loss of his kingdom. Jonathan is the heir and has the most to lose. Yet in verse 4 he hands David his robe and weapons. The chapter repeats that the LORD was with David (verses 12, 14, 28). It also repeats that Saul was afraid (verses 12, 15, 29). Each plan to harm David ends by raising him higher.
A daughter acts against her father's violence

Both of Saul’s children protect David against him. Jonathan does it by argument (verses 4–5). Michal does it by a trick (verses 11–16). In verse 17 Saul calls her husband “my enemy.” Michal shields herself with a lie, and the text does not comment. Saul’s oath in verse 6 lasts only until the next spear (verse 10). In verses 23–24 the Spirit stops him when nothing else has.
Succession makes friendship politically costly

Saul states the matter plainly in verse 31. While David lives, Jonathan will not be king. On the facts Saul is right, and Jonathan already knows it. In verses 14–15 he asks David to spare his family later. He speaks as if David’s rule is certain. His answer to his father in verse 32 is about justice. Saul’s reply is a spear thrown at his own son (verse 33).
Need tests the use of sacred food

Leviticus 24:5–9 reserves this bread for the priests. Ahimelech asks one question about the men’s condition (verse 4). Then he gives the bread, and verse 6 explains that no other was there. The text treats a hungry man’s need as reason enough. Jesus later cites this meal in Matthew 12:3–4. David gained the bread with a false story (verse 2). Verse 7 notes who was watching, and chapter 22 shows the cost.
Royal command does not make every action acceptable

Saul’s order in verse 17 names the victims as “priests of the LORD.” His own guards hear those words and will not strike. Their refusal is silent, and the text records no punishment. Doeg, a foreigner, does what Israelites refuse to do (verse 18). Verse 19 lists men, women, children, and animals. Saul spared such things in Amalek against a command (15:9). David admits in verse 22 that his visit caused these deaths.
Rescue does not guarantee political loyalty

David has just saved Keilah from its enemies (verse 5). Verse 12 says the town would still give him to Saul. The text gives no reason. The fate of Nob in 22:19 was recent, and Keilah had walls to lose. David does not punish or argue; he leaves (verse 13). Saul assumes God has handed David to him (verse 7). David asks instead of assuming, and the answer keeps him alive.
Restraint supplies evidence against an accusation

David’s men and David read the same chance in opposite ways. They see a gift from God (verse 4). He sees a king whom God anointed (verse 6). In verse 11 the piece of robe serves as evidence. He could have killed, and the cloth shows he chose not to. He calls Saul “my father” and leaves judgment to the LORD (verse 12). Saul agrees with every word, yet verse 22 has them go separate ways.
Wisdom stops violence before it gains praise

In chapter 24 David spared a king who hunted him. Here an insult is enough to send him out with swords (verses 21–22). Abigail acts without telling her husband (verse 19). Her case in verses 30–31 looks ahead to David’s rule. A future king should not carry needless bloodshed on his conscience. In verse 33 David admits she stopped him from avenging himself. He credits the LORD with sending her (verse 32).
A second refusal also questions royal protection

David’s words in verse 16 are aimed at Abner, the king’s guard. The missing spear and jar prove how close death came. Saul threw that spear at David in 18:11 and 19:10. David has it in his hand and sends it back (verse 22). His reason is in verses 10–11: the LORD will deal with Saul. Saul’s blessing in verse 25 sounds like peace. In 27:1 David still expects Saul to kill him.
Safety under a patron depends on concealed violence

Verse 11 states David’s reason in plain terms. He leaves no one alive who could report to Gath. The chapter does not say the LORD ordered these raids. David asked the LORD before acting in 23:2 and 23:4. No such question appears here. His safety with Achish rests on a lie (verse 10). Verse 12 shows that Achish is fully deceived.
Saul seeks help from someone his policy endangered

Saul comes for help to a person his own law condemned (verse 3). In verse 9 she fears the visit is a trap. Saul swears by the LORD that she will not be punished (verse 10). He uses God’s name to protect a practice God’s law forbids. The message he receives adds little to chapter 15 (verses 17–18). Only the date is new: tomorrow. The woman he endangered is the one who feeds him (verses 21–25).
Suspicion prevents divided service in battle

David’s lie to Achish has now trapped him. He must fight Israel or betray the king who sheltered him. The commanders’ suspicion in verse 4 opens a way out. They reason that Saul’s former officer could win back favor with Philistine heads. The old song follows David even here (verse 5). The text never says what David meant to do. His protest in verse 8 can be read either way.
Recovery creates a dispute about who deserves a share

Some of the four hundred claim the spoil as their own earnings (verse 22). David answers in verse 23 that the LORD gave it. A gift cannot be divided like wages. Verse 24 therefore gives the guards of the baggage an equal share. Verse 25 says this became a lasting rule in Israel. David also feeds a slave whose master left him to die (verses 11–12). The gifts in verse 26 reach the elders who will soon crown him.
An earlier rescue returns as care for the dead

Jabesh Gilead is the town Saul rescued in chapter 11. That rescue was his first act as king. Now its men cross the Jordan at night into enemy ground (verse 12). They take the bodies from a city wall. They bury the bones and fast (verse 13). The book gives no speech about Saul’s reign at his death. Its last scene of him is the gratitude of people he once saved.
